screens.title: Naming Functions and Methods
screens.narratorSegment: In this short lesson you will learn why function and method names matter more than you might think. Good names act like mini-contracts: they tell other developers what will happen when a function runs and what they can safely rely on. We focus on three practical habits: use verb phrases that describe actions, follow Command-Query Separation so functions either act or return data but not both, and name booleans and constructors so calls read like questions or builders. For example, a name like calculate_average_temperature tells you exactly what to expect, while process_data leaves you guessing. You will also learn to pick descriptive parameter names so calls are readable without comments, and to detect hidden side effects that break the expectations set by a name. By the end of the lesson you will be able to refactor ambiguous methods into clear commands and queries, and choose predicate names that make boolean checks natural. Try to think of naming as part of your A P I design: clearer names reduce time spent reading implementations and prevent subtle bugs. What confusing function name will you refactor first?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Naming Functions and Methods
In this lesson
Why verbs, CQS, and clear parameters

Well-named functions are the verbs of your program. They reduce cognitive load, act as contracts, and make intent explicit without inspecting implementation.

Explore Key Topics

Names are promises. Choose verbs for action, clear prefixes for predicates, and split mixed behavior into commands and queries.

screens.title: Verb Phrase Naming
screens.narratorSegment: A function name should read like an action: it is the verb that tells a reader what will happen when the function runs. Think of names as short sentences: the function call is the verb, and parameters fill the nouns. A name like process_data is generic and forces a reader to open the implementation. By contrast, calculate_average_temperature immediately communicates the algorithmic intent and result type. This clarity matters because it reduces cognitive friction when navigating code and supports better searchability. When deciding a name, ask: what single responsibility does this function have? If the answer lists multiple actions, the function likely needs to be split. Keep names concise but specific. Use domain terms when they add clarity, and avoid unnecessary implementation detail in the name. A function that constructs a new report might be named build_monthly_report, not process_report_stream. A common misconception is that longer names are always bad; long names that precisely state intent are preferable to short ambiguous names. As a concrete check, if you need a comment to explain what the function does, improve the name instead. Takeaway: favor explicit verb phrases that act as a clear contract for callers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Verb Phrase Naming
Definition

Functions should be named with verbs or verb phrases describing a single action and its expected result.

Concrete Example
calculate_average_temperature()
This name communicates the action and the returned value clearly, unlike process_data.
Key Takeaway

Prefer readable verb phrases that reduce the need to inspect implementation.

Common Mistakes & How to Fix
Generic verb: process()
Fix by naming the precise action, e.g., filter_invalid_readings or normalize_sensor_values.
Overlong names that repeat implementation
Trim implementation detail from names; prefer intent over internal steps.
Try this
Inspect a function you recently wrote. If you need a sentence-long comment to explain it, rewrite the function name so that the comment is unnecessary.

screens.title: Command-Query Separation (CQS)
screens.narratorSegment: Command-Query Separation is a simple but powerful guideline: a method should either perform an action that changes system state, or return data without observable side effects. Commands use imperative verb names such as save_user_profile, delete_order, or update_inventory. Queries use names that describe the returned data such as get_user_by_id, fetch_product_details, or calculate_total_price. The purpose is to make side effects explicit. When a query changes state, callers are surprised and code becomes harder to reason about. Consider a function named get_info that also updates last_login. The name promises a pure query, but its behavior is a command as well. That mismatch causes bugs because other code may call it expecting no side effects. To apply CQS, inspect functions for hidden prints, logging, or state changes. If a function both computes and persists results, split it into a pure query that returns values and a command that accepts data to persist. As a concrete example, prefer get_active_users to return a list and log_user_activity as a separate command. Takeaway: names set expectations; keep those expectations honest by separating responsibilities. Command-Query Separation (CQS) means commands change state and use imperative names; queries return data and must not produce side effects. if both exist, split the function.. In practical terms, learn the rule: a method is either a command or a query, not both. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Commands change state and use imperative names; queries return data and must not produce side effects. If both exist, split the function.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Command-Query Separation
Process: Apply CQS
  1. Identify methods that both return data and alter state.
  2. Extract the pure computation into a query named for the returned value.
  3. Create a separate command with an imperative name to perform side effects.
  4. Update call sites so each action is explicit and predictable.
Concrete Example
get_active_users() and log_user_activity()
Split a mixed function into a pure query that returns users and a command that logs an activity.
Anti-pattern
get_users_and_update_status()
Name suggests a query but hides a state change. Rename and split to make behavior explicit.
Check your refactor
  • Does the query return only data and nothing else?
  • Does the command perform side effects and return no data used for further computation?
Key Takeaway

Keep queries free of side effects and name commands imperatively so callers know what to expect.

screens.title: Commands vs Queries — Naming Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Naming patterns help callers infer behavior quickly. Commands often begin with imperative verbs: save, delete, update, log, create. Queries commonly start with get_, fetch_, find_, calculate_, or predicate prefixes like is_, has_, can_ for boolean checks. Using these patterns consistently prevents confusion. Consider a function that tests membership: is_member(user, group) reads like a question and returns a boolean. A common misconception is that get_ is always preferred for queries; in practice use get_ for direct retrieval, fetch_ for operations that may involve remote access or caching semantics, and calculate_ for computed values. Be mindful of inconsistent naming across a codebase—using get_ and fetch_ interchangeably without meaning invites ambiguity. When naming constructors or factory-like functions, choose create_, build_, or make_ so callers understand a new object will be returned. For example, prefer create_user_account over new_user or make_user when explicit behavior matters. The concrete benefit is predictability: consistent prefixes form a small A P I language your team can rely on. Takeaway: adopt clear, consistent prefixes and document any intentional distinctions among them. Commands vs Queries — Naming Patterns means use imperative verbs for commands, get_/fetch_/calculate_ for queries, is_/has_/can_ for predicates, and create_/build_ for object creation.. In practical terms, typical prefixes and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Commands vs Queries — Naming Patterns
Command Prefixes
  • save_user_profile()
  • delete_order()
  • update_inventory()
  • log_activity()
Commands can return success indicators but should not return data for further processing.
Query Prefixes
  • get_user_by_id()
  • fetch_product_details()
  • calculate_total_price()
  • is_admin_user()
Queries should be free of side effects and clearly named for the returned value.
Naming Distinctions
get_
Direct retrieval from a local store.
fetch_
May imply remote access, cache, or I/O behavior.
calculate_
Indicates a computed value, no side effects expected.

screens.title: Parameter Naming
screens.narratorSegment: Parameter names are part of the function’s surface. They tell callers what to pass and make call sites self-documenting. Short or ambiguous parameter names like id or n can be fine in very local contexts, but in most cases you should pick names that describe the expected data and its role. For example, prefer recipient_address and message_body over to and msg in a send_email function. When a parameter represents a complex structure, name it for its intent rather than its type: order_items is clearer than items if the function handles order-specific logic. Good parameter naming reduces the need to look up types or implementation details and prevents misuses like passing the wrong object in the wrong position. A common misconception is that parameter names only matter inside the function; in reality call sites often read parameters inline, so descriptive parameter names improve readability for external callers as well. When refactoring, aim for symmetry: function name, parameter name, and return type should form a clear, cohesive statement of intent. Takeaway: treat parameter names like an A P I surface that communicates expectation and domain meaning.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Parameter Naming
Why it matters

Descriptive parameter names make call sites readable and reduce the need to consult implementation or documentation.

Better:
def send_email(recipient_address, message_body)
Worse:
def send_email(to, msg)
Practical check
  • Does the parameter name describe the role and expected content?
  • Would a caller at a call site understand what to pass without reading the function?
Key Takeaway

Names are part of your API. Choose parameters that make calls self-explanatory.

screens.title: Predicate Naming for Booleans
screens.narratorSegment: Boolean-returning functions are especially interpretable when their names read like questions. Prefixes such as is_, has_, can_, and should_ let the caller write expressions that sound natural and reveal intent. For instance, if user_manager. has_active_subscription(current_user) returns true, the call reads like a direct question. This convention helps both readability and correctness because predicate functions are expected to return only a boolean and not cause state changes. A common mistake is returning non-boolean values or performing side effects inside a predicate, which turns what should be a pure check into an operation with hidden consequences. Another pitfall is ambiguous prefixes; for example, is_ implies a simple state check, while can_ might imply additional computation or permissions checks. When naming predicates, choose the prefix that best matches the question you want to ask. Also, ensure the function's body returns a boolean explicitly and avoids printing, logging, or mutating input data. Concrete example: rename check_active to is_active_user for clarity. Takeaway: predicate names improve clarity and set expectations for purity and return type. Predicate Naming for Booleans means prefix boolean-returning functions with is_/has_/can_/should_ so calls read as questions and indicate purity and boolean return.. In practical terms, name boolean-returning functions like questions using is_, has_, can_, should_. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Predicate Naming for Booleans
Why predicate prefixes help
  • Calls read like questions and document intent.
  • Expectations on return type and purity are clearer.
  • Make tests and conditionals easier to understand.
Examples
is_admin_user(user), has_permission(user, action), can_edit(post, user)
Misuse: A function called is_available that also updates inventory would violate expectations. Keep predicates side-effect free.
Key Takeaway

Name boolean functions as questions and keep them pure. Rename check_active to is_active_user for clarity and predictability.

screens.title: Bad vs Good: Code Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare a problematic example with a clean refactor to see naming and CQS in practice. The bad example has a function that both processes and logs or prints, and it uses vague names and short parameter identifiers. This hides side effects and forces readers to inspect the body. The improved version separates concerns: the pure transformation returns processed data and a separate logging command performs side effects. In the sample, the bad function handle_data may process a list, print a message, and return results. The refactor splits this into process_strings_to_uppercase which returns the transformed list, and log_data_handled which performs the print. The call site becomes explicit: first compute the result, then call the logging command if needed. This pattern makes reasoning about state and testing easier because pure functions are deterministic and commands can be isolated. A common misconception is that combining these actions reduces overhead; in reality it increases coupling and testing cost. Try to spot where side effects occur and move them to clearly named commands. Takeaway: split processing from side effects and pick names that match each function's role.

keyIdea.title: Refactor Pattern
keyIdea.text: Separate transformation from side effects: return data in queries and perform I/O or state changes in commands with imperative names.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Bad vs Good: Code Examples
Bad Example (Violates CQS)
def handle_data(data_list):
    # This function both processes data and returns a result.
    # It might also modify data_list in place.
    processed = [d.upper() for d in data_list]
    print("Data handled.")
    return processed
Good Refactor (Adheres to CQS)
def process_strings_to_uppercase(strings):
    return [s.upper() for s in strings]


def log_data_handled():
    print("Data handled.")
Key Takeaway

Split return-value computations from side effects. Name each function to reflect its single responsibility for easier reasoning and testing.

screens.title: Refactoring UserManager — Starter Code
screens.narratorSegment: Now we apply these naming ideas to the provided UserManager starter. The original class bundles addition, logging, querying, and status checking into methods with terse parameter names like id, n, and a. Our goal is to separate logging from adding users, split get_info into a pure query and a separate command that updates last_login, and turn check_active into a clear predicate. First, rename parameters to descriptive names: user_id, full_name, and active_by_default. Second, extract add_user as a command that performs the insertion and returns a success boolean; move logging into log_user_added as a separate command. Third, create get_user_info as a pure query that returns user data without modifying last_login. Then add update_last_login as a command that explicitly changes state.             print(f"User {n} added.")

        return False

        return None

    def check_active(self, id):
        # Checks if user is active
        user = self.users.get(id)
        return user and user["active"]

screens.narratorSegment: This screen lists recurring mistakes and practical ways to avoid them. First, generic verbs like process, handle, or do_something reveal nothing about intent. fullNarratorScript:
In this short lesson you will learn why function and method names matter more than you might think. Good names act like mini-contracts: they tell other developers what will happen when a function runs and what they can safely rely on. We focus on three practical habits: use verb phrases that describe actions, follow Command-Query Separation so functions either act or return data but not both, and name booleans and constructors so calls read like questions or builders. For example, a name like calculate_average_temperature tells you exactly what to expect, while process_data leaves you guessing. You will also learn to pick descriptive parameter names so calls are readable without comments, and to detect hidden side effects that break the expectations set by a name. By the end of the lesson you will be able to refactor ambiguous methods into clear commands and queries, and choose predicate names that make boolean checks natural. Try to think of naming as part of your A P I design: clearer names reduce time spent reading implementations and prevent subtle bugs. What confusing function name will you refactor first?

In this lesson you will practice four measurable naming skills that improve readability and reduce bugs. First, you will learn to formulate function and method names as clear verbs or verb phrases so that each call explains its purpose without inspecting implementation. For example, prefer calculate_average_temperature over process_data. Second, you will apply Command-Query Separation by identifying when a function performs state changes versus when it only returns data, and then refactor mixed responsibilities into distinct functions. Third, you will identify and avoid common pitfalls like generic verbs, hidden side effects, and inconsistent prefixes. You will see how such names mislead callers and how to detect them. Fourth, you will craft descriptive parameter names and use predicate prefixes like is_, has_, or can_ for boolean-returning functions so calls read like natural questions. Each objective is paired with a short mnemonic or milestone to verify your competency. By the end you should be able to refactor a small class so its methods follow CQS and naming conventions.

This second objectives screen outlines specific takeaways and how you will demonstrate them. You will practice small refactors that make a method’s behavior explicit, splitting a method that both returns data and updates state into a query and a command. You will rename parameters to be explicit about expected inputs and improve call-site readability. You will also rename boolean-returning methods so they read as predicates. For assessment, you will answer diagnostic questions that identify CQS violations and choose better names. An example hands-on task is to refactor a UserManager class so its add, get, and check methods follow CQS and clear parameter naming. During practice you should be able to explain why each new name is better and what hidden side effects were removed or isolated. These activities map directly to the verified competency milestones so you can show a consistent naming habit rather than isolated incidents.

A function name should read like an action: it is the verb that tells a reader what will happen when the function runs. Think of names as short sentences: the function call is the verb, and parameters fill the nouns. A name like process_data is generic and forces a reader to open the implementation. By contrast, calculate_average_temperature immediately communicates the algorithmic intent and result type. This clarity matters because it reduces cognitive friction when navigating code and supports better searchability. When deciding a name, ask: what single responsibility does this function have? If the answer lists multiple actions, the function likely needs to be split. Keep names concise but specific. Use domain terms when they add clarity, and avoid unnecessary implementation detail in the name. A function that constructs a new report might be named build_monthly_report, not process_report_stream. A common misconception is that longer names are always bad; long names that precisely state intent are preferable to short ambiguous names. As a concrete check, if you need a comment to explain what the function does, improve the name instead. Takeaway: favor explicit verb phrases that act as a clear contract for callers.

Command-Query Separation is a simple but powerful guideline: a method should either perform an action that changes system state, or return data without observable side effects. Commands use imperative verb names such as save_user_profile, delete_order, or update_inventory. Queries use names that describe the returned data such as get_user_by_id, fetch_product_details, or calculate_total_price. The purpose is to make side effects explicit. When a query changes state, callers are surprised and code becomes harder to reason about. Consider a function named get_info that also updates last_login. The name promises a pure query, but its behavior is a command as well. That mismatch causes bugs because other code may call it expecting no side effects. To apply CQS, inspect functions for hidden prints, logging, or state changes. If a function both computes and persists results, split it into a pure query that returns values and a command that accepts data to persist. As a concrete example, prefer get_active_users to return a list and log_user_activity as a separate command. Takeaway: names set expectations; keep those expectations honest by separating responsibilities. Naming patterns help callers infer behavior quickly. Commands often begin with imperative verbs: save, delete, update, log, create. Queries commonly start with get_, fetch_, find_, calculate_, or predicate prefixes like is_, has_, can_ for boolean checks. Using these patterns consistently prevents confusion. Consider a function that tests membership: is_member(user, group) reads like a question and returns a boolean. A common misconception is that get_ is always preferred for queries; in practice use get_ for direct retrieval, fetch_ for operations that may involve remote access or caching semantics, and calculate_ for computed values. Be mindful of inconsistent naming across a codebase—using get_ and fetch_ interchangeably without meaning invites ambiguity. When naming constructors or factory-like functions, choose create_, build_, or make_ so callers understand a new object will be returned. Parameter names are part of the function’s surface. They tell callers what to pass and make call sites self-documenting. Short or ambiguous parameter names like id or n can be fine in very local contexts, but in most cases you should pick names that describe the expected data and its role. For example, prefer recipient_address and message_body over to and msg in a send_email function. When a parameter represents a complex structure, name it for its intent rather than its type: order_items is clearer than items if the function handles order-specific logic. Good parameter naming reduces the need to look up types or implementation details and prevents misuses like passing the wrong object in the wrong position. A common misconception is that parameter names only matter inside the function; in reality call sites often read parameters inline, so descriptive parameter names improve readability for external callers as well. When refactoring, aim for symmetry: function name, parameter name, and return type should form a clear, cohesive statement of intent. This screen lists recurring mistakes and practical ways to avoid them. First, generic verbs like process, handle, or do_something reveal nothing about intent. If you encounter such a name, ask what the primary outcome is and rename accordingly. Second, hidden side effects occur when queries change state, for example when a get_ method updates last_login or mutates a passed-in list. Detect these by reviewing the function body for prints, logging, or direct writes to shared structures and move those operations into commands. Third, inconsistent prefixes—mixing get_ and fetch_ without meaning—create a fragile A P I language. Decide on conventions for your project and apply them consistently. Fourth, overloading names to do different things based on parameters can be confusing even when the language allows it; ensure overloaded behaviors still share the same clear intent. As a concrete habit, when you refactor, update call sites and tests so behavior is explicit. A common misconception is that grouping actions inside a single function reduces cognitive load. It often increases it because readers must infer hidden effects. Takeaway: prefer explicit single-responsibility names, separate side effects, and keep naming consistent across the codebase.

These are the essential points to carry forward. First, name functions with verb phrases that communicate a single responsibility. Second, apply Command-Query Separation: queries return data with no side effects, commands perform actions and change state. Third, avoid hidden side effects and generic verbs; they hide intent and increase maintenance cost. Each concept helps you create code that others can read and reason about quickly. Use the predicate prefixes is_, has_, can_, and should_ for boolean-returning functions to make calls read like questions. Name constructors and factory functions with create_, build_, or make_ so it is clear a new object is produced. When you refactor, also pick descriptive parameter names so call sites are self-explanatory. Keep three compact rules in mind as you code. Rule one: name functions as clear verb phrases that state a single responsibility. Rule two: respect Command-Query Separation—queries return data with no side effects, commands perform state changes and use imperative names. Rule three: use descriptive parameter names and predicate prefixes like is_, has_, or can_ for boolean-returning methods. These rules work together: clear names reveal intent, CQS makes side effects explicit, and good parameter naming makes call sites self-documenting. When you adopt these habits, your codebase becomes easier to reason about and simpler to test. As a practical prompt, before you commit, scan changed methods and ask: does this name promise what the code actually does? If not, refactor. That single question will help you keep names honest and your code safer to maintain.
